control_table_comparisons.label:
Conventions

**Creating tools.** Tools are created by script ID (e.g. `TextPlus`, not "Text+"), in one of two ways:

- `comp.AddTool(id)` adds a tool as a user would, for comps the user will see and work on: it is placed in the Node
  Editor automatically and starts from the user's saved default settings, if they have any. The examples use this form.
- `comp.ID()`, for example `comp.Blur()`, or with settings, `comp.FastNoise({'SeetheRate': 0.2, 'XScale': 0.5})`, adds
  a clean tool when layout doesn't matter. It always starts from the tool's built-in defaults, which are the defaults
  given in this reference, and never connects to anything by itself.

Inputs are addressed by their control ID, shown in the `ID` column of each table, which often differs from the label
shown in the Inspector (Text+'s "Tracking" is `CharacterSpacingClone`, for example).

**Auto-connect and auto-merge.** In a comp open in the Fusion page, `AddTool` also connects as the UI does: a new effect
tool connects to the selected tool, and a new generator is merged with it through a new Merge. The new tool then becomes
the selected tool, so a run of `AddTool` calls chains together. The full form is
`comp.AddTool(id, defsettings, x, y, autoconnect, automerge)`. Every argument after `id` is optional, and the flags
default to True: `defsettings` uses the saved defaults, and `autoconnect` and `automerge` connect to the selected tool
(`automerge` overrides the user's auto-merge preference). To add a tool without connecting it, as when the script makes
its own connections, use `comp.AddTool('Blur', True, False, False)`. In current builds the two flags are ignored when a
position is given; alternatively, deselect before each `AddTool` with `comp.SetActiveTool()` (no argument). Comps made
with `fu.NewComp()` have no selection, so nothing auto-connects there.

**Setting values.** In Python, assign to the input as an attribute: `tool.Size = 0.1`. IDs that contain dots
(such as the shape tools' `Translate.X`, or `Transform3DOp.Translate.X` on 3D tools) use item syntax instead:
`tool['Translate.X'] = 0.25`. Reading `tool.Size` gives the
Input object, not its value: read the value at a frame with `tool.Size[frame]` (or `tool['Size'][frame]`), or the
current value with `tool.GetInput('Size')`. `tool.SetInput(id, value)` and
`tool.GetInput(id, frame)` do the same thing for any ID. (In Lua, dotted IDs work directly:
`tool.Translate.X = 0.25`.)

**Value types.**
- *Number*: a float. Checkboxes are 0/1.
- *Combo* and *Multi-button* (`ComboControl`, `MultiButtonControl`): a Number holding the 0-based index of the
  option, in the order listed in the table.
- *ID combo* (`ComboIDControl`, `MultiButtonIDControl`): a string FuID, exactly as listed (e.g. Merge's
  `ApplyMode` takes `"Color Burn"` but `"LinearBurn"`). Copy them exactly (see *Invalid values* below).
- *Point*: `{1: x, 2: y}` or `[x, y]`, read back as `{1: x, 2: y, 3: 0.0}`.
- *Colour*: separate Number inputs per channel, e.g. `Red1`, `Green1`, `Blue1`, `Alpha1`, each 0–1.
- *Text*: a string.
- *Gradient*: colour stops at positions 0–1, created with `comp.Gradient()`:
  `tool.Gradient = comp.Gradient({0.0: [0, 0, 0, 1], 1.0: [1, 0, 0, 1]})` is a black-to-red gradient. Read the stops
  back with `tool.GetInput('Gradient').Value`, which gives `{position: {1: r, 2: g, 3: b, 4: a}}`.
- *Polyline* (a Bézier shape or path: Polygon mask, sPolygon, MultiPoly's Polygon layers, sDuplicate's path, Grid
  Warp, the Planar Tracker's pattern, pEmitter's Bezier region): a dict of points numbered from 1, each
  `{'X': x, 'Y': y}`, with `'Closed': True` added for a closed shape. For example,
  `mask.Polyline = {1: {'X': -0.1, 'Y': -0.1}, 2: {'X': 0.1, 'Y': -0.1}, 3: {'X': 0, 'Y': 0.1}, 'Closed': True}` is a
  triangle. Each point can also have Bézier handles, `LX`, `LY` (towards the previous point) and `RX`, `RY` (towards
  the next), relative to the point. Points without handles get handles of 0, so their segments are straight. The
  points are offsets from the shape's centre: the tool's `Center` on the masks, and the frame centre moved by `Center`
  on the shape tools. A list of points (`[{'X': x, 'Y': y}, ...]`) and `comp.Polyline(points, closed)` work too.
  `tool.GetInput('Polyline')` reads back the same kind of dict, with handles on every point and `'Closed'` only when
  the shape is closed. Polyline inputs are often already animated: see *Animating*.
- *B-spline polyline* (B-Spline mask, sBSpline, MultiPoly's B-Spline layers): made only with
  `comp.BSplinePolyline(points, closed)`, with points as for a Polyline but without handles. A plain dict isn't
  accepted, and leaves the input empty. `tool.GetInput('Polyline')` returns a BSplinePolyline object, which can be
  assigned to another B-spline input as it is. Its `.Value` gives the points and `.Closed` whether it's closed.

**Ranges.** Ranges in the *Default / range* column are the slider range shown in the Inspector (the soft range).
Most inputs accept values outside it, up to hard limits that are usually much wider; the text says so where a
limit matters. For example, Merge `Size` has a 0–5 slider but takes any value above 0. The limits of any input are
in its attributes: `tool.Size.GetAttrs()` gives `INPN_MinScale`/`INPN_MaxScale` (slider) and
`INPN_MinAllowed`/`INPN_MaxAllowed` (hard limits).

**Invalid values.** Setting an invalid value, such as a misspelled ID-combo FuID or a font that isn't installed, is
not an error and reads back as set, but the tool then fails to render: it shows nothing in the viewer, renders
fail, and `tool.Output.GetValue()` returns `None`.

**Use the right type.** Setting an input with a value of the wrong type is not an error, but it leaves the input
empty (reading back `None`) and the tool fails. In particular, some combos and multi-buttons are ID controls that take
FuID strings, and others are Number controls that take an index. The tables say which; from a script, check
`tool.Input.GetAttrs()['INPS_DataType']` (`'FuID'` or `'Number'`).

**Misspelled input IDs** are also silent: `tool.Nope = 1`, `tool['Nope'] = 1` and `tool.SetInput('Nope', 1)` raise no
error and change nothing. Reading an ID that doesn't exist gives `None`, so read a value back after setting it
(`tool.GetInput('XBlurSize')`) when you need to be sure the ID is right.

**Coordinates.** Positions are normalised: `(0, 0)` is the bottom-left of the image, `(1, 1)` is the top-right,
and `(0.5, 0.5)` is the centre, whatever the resolution. Most tools with a normalised Width, Height or Size scale it to the width of the frame, and keep the aspect, so the
same value gives the same proportions at any resolution. Text+ `Size`, for example, is relative to the image width.

**Connecting tools.** `dst.Input = src.Output`, or `dst.Input = src` to connect the tool's default (main)
output, or `dst.ConnectInput('Input', src)`. Read a connection with
`dst.Input.GetConnectedOutput()`. Disconnect with `dst.ConnectInput('Input', None)`.
Output IDs differ between tools, and each section's header line gives them. Mask tools output `Mask`, not `Output`:
`mask.Output` is None, so `tool.EffectMask = mask.Output` disconnects the input without an error. Use
`tool.EffectMask = mask.Mask`, or `tool.EffectMask = mask`. Other tools with differently named outputs include Tween and
Z to World Position (`Image`), Splitter (`Image1`, `Image2`), and the stereo tools, whose dotted outputs connect with item
syntax: `tool['Output.Left']`. When in doubt, connect the tool itself (`dst.Input = src`) to use its main output.

**Animating.** Connect an animation modifier to the input, then set a keyframe with `input[frame] = value`:

```python
tool.Size = comp.BezierSpline()   # or tool.AddModifier('Size', 'BezierSpline')
tool.Size[0] = 0.05               # keyframe at frame 0
tool.Size[24] = 0.10              # keyframe at frame 24

tool.Center = comp.PolyPath()     # Point inputs take a motion path
tool.Center[0] = [0.2, 0.5]
tool.Center[24] = [0.8, 0.5]

shape['Translate.X'] = comp.BezierSpline()   # e.g. an sRectangle's X Offset
shape['Translate.X'][12] = 0.3    # dotted IDs work the same way

tool.Size.ConnectTo(None)         # removes the animation again
```

In Python, use plain values: numbers, strings, `[x, y]` for Points and dicts for Polylines. Values of the Gradient,
B-spline polyline, Image and LookUpTable types are made with constructors on the comp, such as `comp.Gradient({...})`
(see *Value types*). (Lua also has
global value constructors, e.g. `tool.Center[12] = Point(0.8, 0.5)`, `Number(0.3)` and `Text("Hello")`.)

Without a modifier connected, `input[frame] = value` just changes the constant value at every frame, so connect
the spline first. Number inputs use `BezierSpline`. Point inputs use `PolyPath` (the "Path" modifier: a motion path you can see and edit
in the viewer, as in the UI), or `XYPath` for separate X and Y curves. `tool.SetInput(id, value, frame)` sets
keyframes too, and `input[frame] = None` deletes the keyframe at that frame. To list an input's keyframes, ask the
spline connected to it: `tool.Size.GetConnectedOutput().GetTool().GetKeyFrames()`. See BezierSpline for reading and
setting keys with handles. Assigning a plain value to an animated Number or Point input neither removes the animation
nor changes it, so call `ConnectTo(None)` first.

**The initial keyframe.** A spline always holds at least one keyframe, so a newly connected spline starts with one at
the current frame (`comp.CurrentTime`), holding the input's value. On a Number or Point input that keyframe stays when
you set others: connected at frame 50, the example above has keys at 0, 24 and 50, and the value goes back to the old
one at frame 50. Set the first keyframe at the current frame, which replaces it, or delete it with
`tool.Size[comp.CurrentTime] = None`.

**Animated polylines.** The Polyline input of the Polygon and B-Spline masks, sPolygon, sBSpline and MultiPoly's
first layer is already animated when the tool is created, with an initial keyframe at the frame it was added. Set a
shape at a frame with `tool.Polyline[frame] = points`: the first one replaces the initial keyframe. The shape between
keyframes is interpolated point by point, so for a predictable change give every keyframe the same number of points.
A plain assignment, `tool.Polyline = points`, replaces all the keyframes with a single one at the current frame, which
gives a shape that doesn't change. The other Polyline inputs (`Polyline2`, the layers that `AddPolygon` and
`AddBSpline` add to a MultiPoly, sDuplicate's path, Grid Warp, the Planar Tracker's pattern, pEmitter's Bezier region)
are not animated until a `comp.BezierSpline()` is connected. A polyline spline's `GetKeyFrames()` lists the keyframe
times but not their shapes, so read a shape with `tool.GetInput('Polyline', frame)`.

**Modifiers** other than splines attach the same way: `tool.AddModifier('Input', 'ModifierID')`, then reach their
controls with `tool.Input.GetConnectedOutput().GetTool()`. Families are attached by member ID (`PerturbPoint`,
`PublishNumber`, `SwitchNumber`), not by the family name. The Expression modifier connects through its outputs:
`tool.Size = comp.Expression().NumberResult`. See the Modifiers sections.

**Expressions.** `tool.Size.SetExpression('time * 0.01')` sets a formula on an input, in Fusion's Lua expression
syntax. `time` is the current frame, and other tools are named directly (`Transform1.Size * 2`). Read it back with
`GetExpression()`. Clear it with `SetExpression(None)`: an empty string leaves an expression that gives 0, and assigning
a value doesn't remove it. See Expression for more.

**Inspecting a tool.** `tool.SaveSettings()` returns the tool's complete settings as a dict, including every input
value (`settings['Tools']['Blur1']['Inputs']['XBlurSize']`). This is easier than `comp.Copy()`, which goes through the
clipboard. In external Python, the main script must import `OrderedDict` at module level
(`from collections import OrderedDict`); without it, `SaveSettings()` returns `{'Tools': None}`. Importing it inside
a function or in code run with `exec` is not enough. (Fusion's own scripts and Lua don't need this.) The `DaVinciResolveScript` module (in Fusion's own scripts, `bmd`) converts
settings to and from the settings-text form with `writestring(value)` and `readstring(text)`. `comp.Paste(settings)`
creates tools from a settings dict or text. It works in a comp shown in the Fusion page (`fu.CurrentComp`), but not in a
comp made with `fu.NewComp()`. Plain `comp.Paste()` pastes the clipboard text if it's a valid settings table, and
otherwise Fusion's last copied tool. Creating tools from settings can work around API gaps, but only as a last resort.

**Naming.** A tool's name is its ID in the comp, and the comp gives access to it by name: `comp.Text1`,
`comp['Text1']` or `comp.FindTool('Text1')`. Each returns `None` if there's no tool of that name. Default names
(`Text1`, `Merge1`, …) depend on what's already in the comp, so keep the object `AddTool` returns, or give the tool
a name of your own with `tool.SetAttrs({'TOOLB_NameSet': True, 'TOOLS_Name': 'Title'})` and use `comp.Title`
from then on.

## Common Controls

Controls that most tools share. Tool sections only describe their own controls and refer here for these.

### Effect masks

Most image tools have a blue **Effect Mask** input (`EffectMask`). It restricts where the tool has an effect:
inside the mask you get the tool's result, outside it the tool's input passes through unchanged, and soft mask
edges blend between the two. Generators such as Background and Text+ have one too, so a mask also limits where
they draw.

- **Mask tools** (Ellipse Mask, Rectangle Mask, Polygon Mask and the others) create single-channel images for this,
  output as `Mask`. They can be chained: a mask's own `EffectMask` input takes another mask, and the receiving
  (downstream) mask's Paint Mode (`PaintMode`, an ID combo: `"Merge"`, `"Add"`, `"Subtract"`, `"Minimum"`, `"Maximum"`, `"Average"`,
  `"Multiply"`, `"Replace"`, `"Invert"`, `"None"`, `"Ignore"`) sets how the two combine. See Common Controls → Mask tools.
- **Any image can be a mask.** Connect any tool's image output to an `EffectMask` input. Its alpha channel is used
  by default; the Settings tab's `MaskChannel` chooses another (see below), for example 5 for luminance.

Masking one tool with another is a common and powerful way to build effects: a Blur masked by Fast Noise for
patchy defocus, a Color Corrector limited to a soft ellipse, a title revealed by an animated Rectangle Mask. A
Shape-tool graphic can also be given a colour gradient by using it to mask a gradient Background:

```python
star = comp.AddTool('sStar')
shapes = comp.AddTool('sRender')
shapes.Input = star.Output

fill = comp.AddTool('Background')
fill.Type = 'Horizontal'               # left-to-right gradient: TopLeft... to TopRight... colours
fill.TopLeftRed, fill.TopLeftGreen, fill.TopLeftBlue = 1, 0.3, 0
fill.TopRightRed, fill.TopRightGreen, fill.TopRightBlue = 0.6, 0, 1
fill.EffectMask = shapes.Output        # the star's alpha limits the Background to the star shape
```

Background `Type` is an ID multi-button: `"Solid"`, `"Horizontal"` (TopLeft and TopRight colours), `"Vertical"`
(TopLeft and BottomLeft), `"Corner"` (all four corners) or `"Gradient"` (a gradient along `Start`–`End`, shaped by
`GradientType`: `"Linear"`, `"Reflect"`, `"Square"`, `"Cross"`, `"Radial"`, `"Angle"`).

### Settings tab

Found on almost every 2D tool. Tools whose registration leaves out some of these (for example Shape tools, apart
from sRender) don't have them.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Blend | `Blend` | Number | 1 (0–1) | Mixes the tool's result back with its input. 0 passes the input through unchanged, and the tool is skipped. |
| Process when Blend is 0.0 | `ProcessWhenBlendIs00` | Checkbox | 0 | Processes the tool even at Blend 0. |
| Process Red/Green/Blue/Alpha | `ProcessRed` `ProcessGreen` `ProcessBlue` `ProcessAlpha` | Checkbox | 1 | Limits the result to these channels; the others are copied from the input. |
| Apply Mask Inverted | `ApplyMaskInverted` | Checkbox | 0 | Inverts the effect mask. |
| Multiply by Mask | `MultiplyByMask` | Checkbox | 0 | Multiplies the output by the mask, making unmasked areas black/transparent. |
| Fit Mask | `FitMask` | ID combo | `"Crop"` | How a mask of a different size or aspect is fitted: `"Crop"`, `"Stretch"`, `"Inside"`, `"Width"`, `"Height"`, `"Outside"`. |
| Mask Channel | `MaskChannel` | Combo | 3: Alpha | Which channel of an image connected as a mask is used: 0: Red, 1: Green, 2: Blue, 3: Alpha, 4: Hue, 5: Luminance, 6: Saturation, 7: Coverage. |
| Mask Low/High | `MaskLow`, `MaskHigh` | Number | 0, 1 | Remaps the mask range. |
| Use Object / Material | `UseObject`, `UseMaterial`, `ObjectID`, `MaterialID` | Checkbox / Number | 0 | Limits the tool to pixels with the given object or material ID in the image's ID channels (e.g. from Renderer 3D). |
| Motion Blur | `MotionBlur` | Checkbox | 0 | Renders motion blur from the tool's own animated transform. |
| Quality | `Quality` | Number | 2 (0–10) | Motion blur samples either side of the frame. |
| Shutter Angle | `ShutterAngle` | Number | 180 (0–360) | Motion blur length; 360 is a full frame. |
| Center Bias, Sample Spread | `CenterBias`, `SampleSpread` | Number | 0, 1 | Shift and weighting of the motion blur samples, for trail effects. |
| Use GPU | `UseGPU` | Multi-button | 1: Auto (0: Disable, 2: Enable) | GPU processing, for tools that support it. |
| Comments | `Comments` | Text | "" | A note shown on the node. |
| Frame Render Script | `FrameRenderScript` | Text | "" | A Lua script run before the tool renders each frame. |

### Image tab (generators)

Found on tools that create images: Background, Text+, Fast Noise, sRender and other generators. It sets the output
resolution and colour space. By default the comp's frame format is used, which is usually what you want.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Auto Resolution | `UseFrameFormatSettings` | Checkbox | 1 | Uses the comp's frame format for Width, Height and Pixel Aspect. Turn it off to set them yourself. |
| Width, Height | `Width`, `Height` | Number | 1920, 1080 | Output size in pixels, used when Auto Resolution is off. |
| Pixel Aspect | `PixelAspect` | Point | (1, 1) | Pixel aspect ratio. |
| Depth | `Depth` | Multi-button | 0: Default (1: int8, 2: int16, 3: float16, 4: float32) | Bit depth of the output. |
| Color Space Type | `Gamut.ColorType` | ID multi-button | `"Auto"` | `"Auto"` or `"Space"` to tag the output with `Gamut.ColorSpace`. |
| Curve Type | `Gamut.GammaType` | ID multi-button | `"Auto"` | `"Auto"`, `"Space"` (use `Gamut.GammaSpace`) or `"Log"` (use `Gamut.LogType`). |

The global in and out points of a generator (`GlobalIn`, `GlobalOut`) set the frame range over which it produces
images.

### 3D objects

The 3D geometry tools (Shape 3D, Cube 3D, Image Plane 3D, Camera 3D, Locator 3D, Point Cloud 3D and others) share
three tabs of controls: **Transform**, **Controls** and **Material**. Their sections in this reference only describe
their own controls and refer here. Text 3D is a partial exception: it has the Transform tab, but its Shading tab
replaces the Controls and Material tabs.

Most of these controls are dotted IDs. Set them with item syntax, as with `tool['Translate.X']` in 2D tools:

```python
cube = comp.AddTool('Cube3D')
cube['Transform3DOp.Translate.X'] = 0.5
cube['Transform3DOp.Rotate.Y'] = 30
cube['SurfaceCubeInputs.Visibility.IsVisible'] = 1
```

Geometry tools output a 3D scene (`DataType3D`, output `Output`), which must be connected to a Merge 3D and then to a
Renderer 3D to become an image. Their 3D controls are only effective within a scene that reaches a Renderer 3D.

#### Transform tab

Positions the object in the scene. The same controls appear on Merge 3D, Transform 3D and Camera 3D,
where they move everything connected to them.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Translation | `Transform3DOp.Translate.X`, `Transform3DOp.Translate.Y`, `Transform3DOp.Translate.Z` | Number | 0 (X, Y: −2 to 2; Z: −10 to 10) | Position in scene units. |
| Rotation | `Transform3DOp.Rotate.X`, `Transform3DOp.Rotate.Y`, `Transform3DOp.Rotate.Z` | Number | 0 (−180 to 180 degrees) | Rotation about each axis. |
| Rotation Order | `Transform3DOp.Rotate.RotOrder` | ID combo | `"XYZ"` | Order the three rotations are applied: `"XYZ"`, `"XZY"`, `"YXZ"`, `"YZX"`, `"ZXY"`, `"ZYX"`. |
| Pivot | `Transform3DOp.Pivot.X`, `Transform3DOp.Pivot.Y`, `Transform3DOp.Pivot.Z` | Number | 0 (−2 to 2) | Point the rotation and scale turn about. |
| Scale | `Transform3DOp.Scale.X`, `Transform3DOp.Scale.Y`, `Transform3DOp.Scale.Z` | Number | 1 (0.001 to 5) | Size along each axis. |
| Lock X/Y/Z | `Transform3DOp.ScaleLock` | Checkbox | 1 | Scales all three axes together. |
| Use Target | `Transform3DOp.UseTarget` | Checkbox | 0 | The object always rotates to face the Target point below. |
| Target | `Transform3DOp.Target.X`, `Transform3DOp.Target.Y`, `Transform3DOp.Target.Z` | Number | 0 | The point to aim at when Use Target is on. |
| Invert Transform | `Transform3DOp.InvertTransform` | Checkbox | 0 | Applies the inverse of the transform. Useful for matching tracker data. |
| Import Transform | `Transform3DOp.Import` | Button | | Loads a transform from a file. |

#### Controls tab

Per-object visibility, lighting, matte and blending. The IDs below are shown for Shape 3D's plane, which is the
`SurfacePlaneInputs` prefix; the other primitives use their own prefix (`SurfaceCubeInputs`, `SurfaceSphereInputs` and
so on). Image Plane 3D uses `SurfacePlaneInputs`. Camera 3D and Locator 3D use the same suffixes without a shape prefix.

| Control | ID suffix | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Visible | `Visibility.IsVisible` | Checkbox | 1 | Shows the object. Turn off to hide it without disconnecting it. |
| Unseen by Cameras | `Visibility.IsUnseenByCameras` | Checkbox | 0 | Hides the object from the cameras. |
| Cull Front Face / Back Face | `Visibility.CullFrontFace`, `Visibility.CullBackFace` | Checkbox | 0 | Removes the front or back faces of the surface. |
| Suppress Aux Channels for Transparent Pixels | `Visibility.DiscardTransparentPixels` | Checkbox | 1 | Leaves the auxiliary channels (Z, Normal, ObjectID and so on) empty where the object is transparent. |
| Affected by Lights | `Lighting.IsAffectedByLights` | Checkbox | 1 | The object responds to lights in the scene. |
| Shadow Caster | `Lighting.IsShadowCaster` | Checkbox | 1 | The object casts shadows. |
| Shadow Receiver | `Lighting.IsShadowReceiver` | Checkbox | 1 | The object shows shadows cast on it. |
| Is Matte | `Matte.IsMatte` | Checkbox | 0 | Makes the object a matte: it hides what is behind it but is otherwise invisible. Use it for shadow catchers and occluders. |
| Opaque Alpha | `Matte.OpaqueAlpha` | Checkbox | 0 | Makes a matte fully opaque in the alpha channel. |
| Infinite Z | `Matte.InfiniteZ` | Checkbox | 1 | Treats a matte as infinitely far away, so other objects always appear in front of it. |
| Hardware blend | `BlendMode.GL.BlendMode` | ID combo | `"Additive"` | Blend mode for the OpenGL renderer: `"Additive"`, `"Subtractive"`, `"Accumulate"`, `"Replace"`, `"TransMatte"`, `"SolidMatte"`. |
| Software blend | `BlendMode.SW.BlendMode` | ID combo | `"Additive"` | Blend mode for the software renderer, with the usual layer modes (`"Normal"`, `"Screen"`, `"Multiply"` and so on). |
| Software operator | `BlendMode.SW.Operator` | ID combo | `"Over"` | Porter-Duff operator, as on Merge: `"Over"`, `"In"`, `"Held Out"` and so on. |
| Subtractive/Additive | `BlendMode.SW.SubtractiveAdditive` | Number | 1 (0–1) | As on Merge. |
| Gain, Burn In | `BlendMode.SW.Gain`, `BlendMode.SW.BurnIn` | Number | 1, 0 | As on Merge. |
| Clamp Coverage | `BlendMode.SW.ClampCoverage` | Checkbox | 1 | Clamps the coverage value. Not documented in the manual. |
| Object ID | `ObjectID.ObjectID` | Number | 1 (1–30) | The ID written to the ObjectID channel of the Renderer 3D, and used by Override 3D to select objects. The registered default is 65535, but a new instance reads 1. |
| Show Normals | `Controls.Normals.Show` | Checkbox | 0 | Draws the surface normals in the viewer. |
| Scale (normals) | `Controls.Normals.Scale` | Number | 1 (0–10) | Length of the displayed normals. |
| Show Tangents | `Controls.Tangents.Show` | Checkbox | 0 | Draws the surface tangents in the viewer. |
| Wireframe | `Wireframe` | Checkbox | 0 | Draws the mesh as wireframe in the OpenGL viewer and renderer. |
| Wireframe Antialiasing | `IsWireframeAntialiased` | Checkbox | 1 | Smooths the wireframe lines. |

Object IDs are the way to pick out one object in a render: a Renderer 3D with ObjectID enabled writes the IDs into
its own channels (see Renderer 3D), and Common Controls → Settings tab `UseObject` and `ObjectID` limit a 2D tool to
pixels with a given ID.

#### Material tab

The surface appearance. These controls are the basic material, used unless a material is connected to the object's
`MaterialInput` (see 3D materials and textures, for Material nodes such as Blinn, Phong and OpenPBR).

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Diffuse Red, Green, Blue | `MtlStdInputs.Diffuse.Color.Red`, `MtlStdInputs.Diffuse.Color.Green`, `MtlStdInputs.Diffuse.Color.Blue` | Number | 1 (0–1) | Base colour. |
| Alpha | `MtlStdInputs.Diffuse.Color.Alpha` | Number | 1 (0–1) | Colour alpha. |
| Opacity | `MtlStdInputs.Diffuse.Opacity` | Number | 1 (0–1) | Opacity of the surface. |
| Specular Red, Green, Blue | `MtlStdInputs.Specular.Color.Red`, `MtlStdInputs.Specular.Color.Green`, `MtlStdInputs.Specular.Color.Blue` | Number | 1 (0–1) | Highlight colour. |
| Intensity | `MtlStdInputs.Specular.Intensity` | Number | 1 (0–1) | Highlight strength. |
| Exponent | `MtlStdInputs.Specular.Exponent` | Number | 50 (1–100) | Highlight sharpness. Higher is smaller and glossier. |
| Transmittance colour | `MtlStdInputs.Transmittance.Color.Red`, `MtlStdInputs.Transmittance.Color.Green`, `MtlStdInputs.Transmittance.Color.Blue` | Number | 0 | Colour that light passing through the surface takes on. |

The object's `MaterialInput` (`MtlGraph3D`) is a green input for a 3D material. Connecting one replaces the basic
material above. On Image Plane 3D, the same input also takes a 2D image, which is used as the diffuse texture.

### 3D materials and textures

Materials and textures are the same kind of tool. Each one outputs a material (`MaterialOutput`, type Material Output),
and each material tool has inputs that accept another material. Connect the finished material into the material input
of a geometry tool, such as `FrontMaterialInput` on Cube 3D, or the material input of the other geometry tools. A texture
is then a material that feeds one of the inputs of another material. This is how a shader is built up: a texture
(Fast Noise Texture, Gradient, Bump Map and so on) feeds a material (Blinn, Phong, Cook-Torrance, OpenPBR and so on),
which feeds the geometry.

A 2D image can be connected to most material inputs, in place of a texture. The manual says that the material then uses
the image as a basic diffuse texture. Image inputs on the texture tools (Texture 2D, Bump Map, Cube Map and so on) take
images directly.

**How a texture combines with a control.** In each material, a texture on an input multiplies the matching control. For
example, `Diffuse.Color.Material` is multiplied by the Diffuse Color controls, and a texture on `Specular.Exponent.Material`
scales the Specular Exponent. When no texture is connected, the multiplier is 1, so the control's value applies on its
own. Colour inputs use the texture's colour channels, and scalar inputs use the channel named in the manual (usually
alpha). Where the manual and the source disagree on the channel, the source is what the tool does. See the notes in each
material for the exceptions.

**Shared controls.** The Blinn, Phong, Cook-Torrance and Ward materials share these controls. Each material's section
lists only its own primary controls.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Diffuse Color | `Diffuse.Color.Red`, `Green`, `Blue` | Number | 1, 1, 1 (0–1) | Base colour of the surface. Multiplied by the Diffuse Color texture. |
| Diffuse Alpha | `Diffuse.Color.Alpha` | Number | 1 (0–1) | Alpha of the surface. Multiplied by the alpha of the Diffuse texture. |
| Opacity | `Diffuse.Opacity` | Number | 1 (0–1) | Transparency of the surface. Reduces the colour and alpha of both diffuse and specular. |
| Transmittance Colour | `Transmittance.Color.Red`, `Green`, `Blue` | Number | 0, 0, 0 (0–1) | Colour of light passing through the surface, which tints its cast shadow. (1, 1, 1) transmits everything. |
| Alpha Detail | `Transmittance.AlphaDetail` | Number | 1 (0–1) | 0 makes the whole object cast a shadow. 1 lets the alpha channel decide which parts cast one. |
| Color Detail | `Transmittance.ColorDetail` | Number | 0 (0–1) | Brings the diffuse colour and texture colour into the transmitted shadow colour. |
| Transmittance Saturation | `Transmittance.Saturation` | Number | 1 (0–1) | Saturation of the transmitted colour. 0 gives monochrome shadows. |
| Receives Lighting | `ReceivesLighting` | Checkbox | 1 | Off makes the surface fully lit, ignoring the scene's lights. |
| Receives Shadows | `ReceivesShadows` | Checkbox | 1 | Off stops the surface from being shadowed. |
| Two Sided Lighting | `UseTwoSidedLighting` | Checkbox | 0 | Adds normals facing the other way on the back, so the back is lit correctly. Use it for planes and open geometry. |
| Enable PBR Material | `EnablePBRMaterial` | Checkbox | 0 | Shades the material with the physically based (GGX) model, which converts the material's settings to the PBR model. Applies to Blinn, Phong, Cook-Torrance and Ward. |
| Material ID | `MaterialID` | Number | 1 or 2 on a new tool (slider 1–30) | Identifies the material. The value goes into the MatID channel when Renderer 3D's MatID option is on. |

The Bump Map input (`Bumpmap.Material`) takes only a Bump Map (or another material that gives normals). It uses the
RGB channels as texture-space normals. The Bump Map tool produces that material from an image.

**Notes on the Material ID.** A new material starts with a small ID (for example 1 or 2), not the registered 65535.
Giving each material a different ID lets the MatID channel tell them apart in compositing.

### Deep images

A **deep image** keeps several samples for each pixel instead of one. Each sample holds a colour, an alpha and a depth (Z). Where two objects overlap in a pixel, both are kept at their own depths, so a deep image can be re-sorted in depth. A normal image keeps only the result that is visible. Deep images are usually EXR files rendered with deep data (Renderer 3D can output them, and Loader and MediaIn read them). Deep compositing needs a linear colour space: convert to linear before the deep tools, and convert back after the image is flattened.

The deep tools fit together like this:

- **Image To Deep** (`ImageToDeep`) gives a 2D image a single sample per pixel, at a depth you set. It is how a plate, graphic or 2D element joins a deep comp.
- **dMerge** (`dMerge`) combines deep images. Its Background is the base, and each Foreground adds its samples, sorted by depth.
- **dHoldout** (`dHoldout`) cuts a deep Background where a deep Foreground is in front of it.
- **Deep To Image** (`DeepToImage`) flattens a deep image into an ordinary 2D image, for Merge, Saver or any 2D tool.
- The other deep tools (dCrop, dResize, dTransform, dRecolor, dColor Corrector) act on the samples. Each also accepts a 2D image and converts it to deep automatically. Only Image To Deep and Deep To Image do not.

Deep images carry extra channels, called aux channels, that the 2D and Deep Pixel tools read. Renderer 3D decides which ones it writes, and its output channels must include them (the Deep Pixel chapter of the manual, for example, requires Z-Depth and Normals for Ambient Occlusion):

| Channel | Read or written by |
|---|---|
| Z (depth) | Depth Blur, Fog, Ambient Occlusion; Z To Disparity and Disparity To Z (stereo); Z To WorldPos |
| Normals | Ambient Occlusion, Shader |
| UV | Texture |
| World position (XYZ) | Volume Fog, Volume Mask, Z To WorldPos |
| Vector and Back Vector | Optical Flow writes them; Vector Motion Blur, Vector Denoise, Vector Transform, Vector Warp and Smooth Motion read them |
| Disparity | Disparity writes it; Smooth Motion, Disparity To Z and New Eye read it |
| Object and Material IDs | The Use Object and Use Material settings on most image tools |

Repair Frame and Tween compute their own motion, and New Eye and Stereo Align work on the eyes directly. All four destroy the aux channels of their input rather than passing them on (the manual says so for each), so add another Disparity or Optical Flow node after them if the channels are needed again.

### Krokodove tools

Krokodove tools share several groups of controls. The tool sections describe only their own controls and refer here for these. Which groups a tool has depends on its category, as the comparison below shows.

**Page by category.** The Common page is on every Krokodove tool. Shape and image tools also have UseGPU. The Settings page is on the image tools only. The Style page is on the styled shape tools and the shape generators. Transform pages are on the shape generators and the region tools.

| Control group | Shape | Shape Create | Region | Image (for example KD_Duplicate) | 3D (for example KD_Kill3D) |

| Common page (Comments, render scripts, HideInputs, ProcessLayers) | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| UseGPU (Common page) | yes | yes | no | yes | no |
| Settings page (Blend, channels, masks) | no | no | no | yes | no |
| Style page | 6 styled tools | 3 | no | no | no |
| Transform page | no | Shape prefix | Transform prefix | no | no |
| Invert | no | no | yes | no | no |

### Mask tools

The mask tools are Bitmap, B-Spline, Ellipse, Mask Paint, MultiPoly, Polygon, Ranges, Rectangle, Triangle and Wand.
They all share the controls below. Their Settings tab has only the motion blur, GPU, layer, comment and script
controls. The blend and channel controls of 2D tools (Blend, Process Red/Green/Blue/Alpha, Multiply by Mask and so on)
are not there, because a mask outputs a single-channel `Mask`. For how masks are used and chained, see Effect masks
above.

**Controls tab**

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Show View Controls | `ShowViewControls` | Checkbox | 1 | Shows the mask's onscreen controls (centre, points, angle) in the viewer. Turning it off hides them without changing the mask. |
| Level | `Level` | Number | 1 (0–1) | Transparency of the whole mask. 1 is opaque (apart from soft edges). Lower values make it partly transparent, like lowering a Blend. |
| Filter | `Filter` | ID combo | `"Fast Gaussian"` | The filter used to soften the edge: `"Box"` (fastest, least smooth), `"Bartlett"`, `"Multi-box"` (uses Num Passes), `"Gaussian"` and `"Fast Gaussian"`. |
| Soft Edge | `SoftEdge` | Number | 0 (0–0.2) | Feathers the edge with Filter. 0 gives a crisp edge; higher values fade well beyond the shape. |
| Num Passes | `Passes` | Number | 4 (1–16) | Number of passes for the `"Multi-box"` filter. From 4 up it is close to Gaussian, with no ringing. |
| Border Width | `BorderWidth` | Number | 0 (−0.2 to 0.2) | Grows (positive) or shrinks (negative) a solid shape. With Solid off, the outline is this thick, so it needs a value above 0 to show. |
| Paint Mode | `PaintMode` | ID combo | `"Merge"` | How this mask combines with the mask on its `EffectMask` input: `"Merge"`, `"Add"`, `"Subtract"`, `"Minimum"`, `"Maximum"`, `"Average"`, `"Multiply"`, `"Replace"`, `"Invert"`, `"None"` or `"Ignore"`. Only matters when an `EffectMask` is connected. |
| Invert | `Invert` | Checkbox | 0 | Inverts the whole mask, including the areas the shape doesn't cover. |
| Solid | `Solid` | Checkbox | 1 | On: the shape is filled. Off: only its outline is drawn, `BorderWidth` thick. Hidden and unused on Bitmap, Ranges and Wand masks. |

Paint Mode is set on the downstream mask, the one whose `EffectMask` the other mask is connected to, and combines that
mask with the upstream one: with `"Subtract"`, the downstream mask is subtracted from the upstream one. The first mask
in a chain has no upstream mask, so its Paint Mode has no visible effect. Paint Mode is a string, so set it as
`mask.PaintMode = "Subtract"`; an index such as `7` leaves it empty (reading back `None`) and the mask fails to render.

| Process Mode | `ProcessMode` | ID combo | `"FullFrames"` | `"FullFrames"`, `"NTSC"`, `"PAL"`, `"PALReversed"` or `"NTSCReversed"`. Leave it at `"FullFrames"` unless you are working with fields. |

| Pixel Aspect | `PixelAspect` | Point | (1, 1) | Pixel aspect ratio of the mask. |

| Depth | `Depth` | Multi-button | 0: Default (1: int8, 2: int16, 3: float16, 4: float32) | Bit depth of the mask. |
| Clipping Mode | `ClippingMode` | ID multi-button | `"None"` | `"Frame"` uses the whole frame as the area the mask is defined over, so soft edges aren't cut off at the edges of the input. `"None"` doesn't clip to the input's area. |

### Particle tools

Particle tools pass a particle system from node to node. Every tool except pRender takes and gives `Particles`, so the
chain is: a source (pEmitter or pImageEmitter), then any number of forces, styles and limiters, then pRender, which
turns the particles into an image or 3D geometry. A particle tool does nothing by itself, and its result shows only once
it reaches pRender. The controls below appear on most particle tools; each tool's section lists only what it adds.

**Random Seed** (`RandomSeed`, Number 0–1000) selects a random sequence, `Randomize` (Button) reseeds it, and `TimeLockSeed`
(Checkbox) keeps the same random values from frame to frame. Tools without randomness, such as pKill, don't have these.

**Conditions tab.** These limit which particles a tool affects. They apply in addition to the Region.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | `Probability` | Number | 1 (0–1) | The chance that a particle is affected on each frame. 0.6 gives a 60 per cent chance. |
| Start Age | `StartAge` | Number | 0 (0–1) | The start of the part of each particle's life the tool affects, as a fraction of its lifespan. |
| End Age | `EndAge` | Number | 1 (0–1) | The end of that part. For the last 20 per cent of life, use Start Age 0.8 and End Age 1. |
| Set Mode | `SetMode` | ID combo | `"Ignore"` | `"Ignore"` (all particles), `"Affect"` (only particles in the Set checkboxes that are on), `"DontAffect"` (only particles in the Set checkboxes that are off). |
| Sets | `Set1` … `Set32` | Checkbox | 1 (force tools), 0 (emitters) | On the emitters and pSpawn (`NewSet1`…), the sets given to new particles. On the other tools, the sets that Set Mode tests. |

Set Mode doesn't hide the Set checkboxes when it changes; they are always visible, and only take effect when Set Mode is
`"Affect"` or `"DontAffect"`.

**Region tab.** The region is the shape that a tool uses. pEmitter uses it to decide where particles are born; other
tools use it to limit where they act. Its shape is set by `Region` and the controls for that shape are listed below.

Not on pEmitter, pImageEmitter, pAvoid or pBounce, which have their own region behaviour. |

| Size Over Life | `ParticleStyle.SizeOverLife` | LookUpTable | none | Size multiplier over the life, as a spline. |
| Fade In, Fade Out | `ParticleStyle.FadeIn`, `ParticleStyle.FadeOut` | Number (range) | 0 and 1 | The part of life over which the particle fades in and out. |
| Subtractive/Additive | `ParticleStyle.SubtractiveAdditive` | Number | 1 (0–1) | Compositing with the image behind, as on Merge. |
| Blur [2D] | `ParticleStyle.Blur`, `BlurVariance`, `BlurOverLife`, `ZBlurDOF`, `BlurNearZ`, `BlurFarZ`, `BlurBlend` | Number | 0 | A 2D blur of each particle. `ZBlurDOF` with Near and Far blurs particles by their Z depth instead. |
| Glow [2D] | `ParticleStyle.Glow` | Number | 0 (0–1) | A glow around each particle in 2D. |

### Scripting particle controls

Set and read them as for any other tool. Dotted IDs use item syntax:

```python
em = comp.AddTool('pEmitter')
em.Region = 'SphereRgn'
em['SphereRgn.Size'] = 0.2
em.Style = 'ParticleStyleBitmap'
em['ParticleStyle.Size'] = 0.05
```

Keep in mind that a particle tool's controls take effect only in the mode they belong to; set the Region and Style
first, then the values for that mode.

### USD tools

The USD tools (the USD category: uLoader, uShape, uMerge, uCamera, the uLights, uRenderer and the rest) are a separate scene
system from the classic 3D tools in this reference (Shape 3D, Merge 3D, Renderer 3D). They share the same 3D ideas (objects,
cameras, lights, transforms) but not the data. The USD tools pass a **USD scene** (data type `USD`, a stage of prims), and
classic 3D tools pass a **3D scene** (`DataType3D`). USD tools accept classic 3D scenes, geometry and materials and
convert them to USD, but not the reverse: a USD output can't go into a Merge 3D or a Renderer 3D input, and the
connection is refused. Texture tools (uTexture, uTextureTransform, uNormalMap) pass a `USDTexture`,
and the uRenderer outputs an ordinary `Image`, so its output merges like any other image.

**Typical chain.** Scene elements come from a uLoader (an imported `.usd`, `.usda`, `.usdc` or `.usdz` file) or are made with a
uShape. They are combined in a uMerge with a uCamera and any uLights. The uMerge goes to a uRenderer, which flattens the scene
to an image, and a 2D Merge puts that image over the video. Every USD scene must end in a uRenderer before it reaches the
2D compositing tools. Verified connections for this chain (values and connections only, no render):

```python
video = comp.AddTool('Background')            # stand-in for the plate

cam = comp.AddTool('uCamera')
cam.FocalLength = 50
cam['USDXf.Translate.Z'] = 5                  # 5 units back from the origin

key = comp.AddTool('uDistantLight')
key.Intensity = 1.0
key['USDXf.Rotate.X'] = -45

ball = comp.AddTool('uShape')
ball.Shape = 'USDGeomSphere'
ball['USDGeomSphere.Radius'] = 0.5
ball['USDMtlInputs.Diffuse.DiffuseRed'] = 0.9
ball['USDMtlInputs.Diffuse.DiffuseGreen'] = 0.4
ball['USDMtlInputs.Diffuse.DiffuseBlue'] = 0.1

merge = comp.AddTool('uMerge')
merge.SceneInput1 = ball.Output
merge.SceneInput2 = cam.Output
merge.SceneInput3 = key.Output

render = comp.AddTool('uRenderer')
render.SceneInput = merge.Output
render.Lighting = 'Scene'                     # use the lights in the scene

over = comp.AddTool('Merge')
over.Background = video.Output
over.Foreground = render.Output
```

**The shared Transform tab.** Most USD tools have a Transform tab with the same controls (uLoader,
uExport, uRenderer, uSwitch, uShader, uMaterialX, uTexture, uReplaceMaterial and uVisibility have none). The IDs are dotted, so set them with
item syntax, as in the chain above. On a uMerge the transform moves every connected element together, which is how parenting
works in USD. On the other tools it moves that one object or prim set.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Translation | `USDXf.Translate.X`, `USDXf.Translate.Y`, `USDXf.Translate.Z` | Number | 0 (X, Y: −2 to 2; Z: −10 to 10) | Position. |
| Rotation | `USDXf.Rotate.X`, `USDXf.Rotate.Y`, `USDXf.Rotate.Z` | Number | 0 (−180 to 180 degrees) | Rotation about each axis. |
| Rotation Order | `USDXf.Rotate.RotOrder` | ID combo | `"XYZ"` | Order the rotations are applied: `"XYZ"`, `"XZY"`, `"YXZ"`, `"YZX"`, `"ZXY"`, `"ZYX"`. |
| Pivot | `USDXf.Pivot.X`, `USDXf.Pivot.Y`, `USDXf.Pivot.Z` | Number | 0 (−2 to 2) | Point the rotation and scale turn about. |
| Scale | `USDXf.Scale.X`, `USDXf.Scale.Y`, `USDXf.Scale.Z` | Number | 1 (0.001 to 5) | Size along each axis. |
| Lock X/Y/Z | `USDXf.ScaleLock` | Checkbox | 1 | Scales all three axes together. |
| Use Target | `USDXf.UseTarget` | Checkbox | 0 | The object turns to face the target point. |
| Target | `USDXf.Target.X`, `USDXf.Target.Y`, `USDXf.Target.Z` | Number | 0 | The point to aim at when Use Target is on. |
| Invert Transform | `USDXf.InvertTransform` | Checkbox | 0 | Applies the inverse of the transform. |

**Prim selection.** Tools that act on part of a scene (uTransform, uVisibility, uVariant, uReplaceMaterial, and the cameras and
lights for their own prim) have a Prim Selection control. Its **Pick** button opens the USD Scene Tree dialog, where prims are
chosen. From a script, the chosen prims are the text list `SelectedPrims`, and `InvertPrimSelection` (checkbox, 0) inverts the
choice. The prim-path format from script was not tested, so the script examples leave prim selection alone.

**Visibility.** The only visibility control is on uVisibility (`VisibilityOverride`, "Visible"), which hides or shows the
selected prims. Other tools have no separate visibility control, so hide a whole object by disconnecting it or by using
uVisibility.

**Export as Separate Stage** (`SeparateStage`, Checkbox, 0) appears on most USD tools. It is not described in the manual; its
effect was not tested.

**Image inputs.** Tools with an Image input (uImagePlane, uTexture, uShape's diffuse image, uDomeLight, uCamera's image
plane, uProjector) take a 2D image from any Fusion node. When an image is connected, the matching File Name control is hidden.

**How it differs from the classic 3D chain.**
- *Data.* USD tools use `USD`, `USDTexture` and `Image` outputs. Classic tools use `DataType3D`. USD inputs accept classic
  3D scenes, geometry and materials and convert them (a Shape 3D into a uMerge, for example), but a Merge 3D or Renderer 3D
  refuses a USD output. The camera and mesh inputs of a uRenderer (`CameraInput`) and a uDuplicate (`MeshInput`) also take
  classic 3D outputs.
- *Cameras and lights.* A uCamera or uLight only acts on the geometry in the same uMerge, as with Merge 3D. The USD
  lights (uDistant, uDome, uRect and so on) have their own shadow controls for each light.
- *Renderer.* uRenderer has one renderer type, Storm, and works from the uMerge output. The classic Renderer 3D offers
  Software and OpenGL renderers (see Renderer 3D).
- *Materials.* USD objects take materials from uShape's Material tab, uShader (USD or MaterialX models), uMaterialX and
  uReplaceMaterial. They don't use the classic Material tabs (see the classic material sections).

**See also:** uLoader, uMerge, uRenderer, uCamera, uShape, uTransform, uReplace Material, uShader, Merge 3D, Renderer 3D, Merge.
